The coronavirus will weigh on near-term U.S. activity and elevate downside risks to the outlook. However, the Committee’s rapid move to the effective lower bound alongside large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, expanded repo operations, discount-window support, capital/liquidity buffer relief, and dollar swap lines is consistent with the credit-channel literature and liquidity-trap insights that such measures can cushion aggregate demand and stabilize market functioning. Empirical work on credit frictions shows that easing external finance premia helps support investment and smaller firms (Bernanke–Gertler; Gertler & Gilchrist 1994; Kashyap, Lamont & Stein 1994; Oliner & Rudebusch 1996a), while VAR evidence finds monetary shocks materially affect output (Christiano, Eichenbaum & Evans; Sims). With market-based inflation compensation having fallen and survey expectations little changed, maintaining an accommodative stance is aligned with inflation-forecast targeting principles (Svensson 1997) and with balance-sheet policy at the zero lower bound (e.g., term-structure/shadow-rate evidence in Rudebusch & Wu 2008). Netting these considerations, the near-term tone remains negative due to the pandemic shock, but literature-based priors suggest the announced measures materially attenuate the downturn and deflation risk.
